questions.question: An alarm sounds and nobody knows whether it is a drill. How should you treat it?

options.text: As a drill until someone confirms a real fire
As real until it is officially confirmed otherwise
As real only if you can smell smoke

questions.why: The guide says to treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise.

questions.question: During a fire, the elevator is a safe way to move people who walk slowly.
questions.why: Elevators can stop or fill with smoke. The guide says not to use them during a fire; use the stairs.

questions.question: Which of these belong to the guide's advice when an alarm sounds? Select all that apply.

options.text: Collect documents from your desk first
Use the stairs, not the elevator
Take only what you can carry in a few seconds

questions.why: The guide asks you to stop non-essential tasks, use the stairs and take only what you can carry in seconds. Collecting documents delays the exit.

questions.question: Someone needs help to leave, but helping them is not safe. What should you report to responders?
questions.why: The guide says to help only if it is safe; otherwise report the person's location so responders can reach them.

questions.question: What part of your hand do you use to check whether a closed door is hot?
questions.why: The guide says to feel a closed door with the back of your hand before opening it.

questions.question: A door on your route feels hot. What does the guide tell you to do?

options.text: Do not open it and use another route
Open it fully to let the heat out

questions.why: A hot door suggests fire behind it. Do not open it; use another route.

questions.question: Put the steps for going through a closed door in the guide's order.

items.text: Open it slowly, ready to close it at once
Feel the door with the back of your hand
Close it behind you once you are through
If it is cool, go on to open it

questions.why: Check the door first, open a cool door slowly so you can shut it again, and close doors behind you to slow fire and smoke.

questions.question: Why does the guide tell you to stay low in smoke?

options.text: Smoke and hot gases rise, so the air is cleaner near the floor
It is easier to find the exit signs

questions.why: Smoke and hot gases rise, so the cleaner air is near the floor.

questions.question: Breaking a window helps clear smoke from a corridor.
questions.why: Extra air can make a fire grow, and it will not clear your route. The guide says not to break windows to clear smoke.

questions.question: Your route is blocked by smoke. Which actions does the guide list? Select all that apply.

options.text: Go to a room with a window
Close the door and seal gaps if you can
Signal your position and call the emergency number

questions.why: If your route is blocked, go to a room with a window, close the door, seal gaps, signal and call. Running through smoke exposes you to the worst air.

questions.question: While moving through smoke, what does the guide suggest you keep on the wall?
questions.why: Keeping one hand on the wall helps you hold your direction when you cannot see well.

questions.question: Where should the assembly point be?

options.text: Away from the building and its entrances
In the car park next to the doors

questions.why: Away from the building and its entrances, so responders have access.

questions.question: Once you are out, you may go back in to fetch a colleague if the smoke looks light.
questions.why: The guide says not to re-enter the building until responders declare it safe.

questions.question: At the assembly point, what two things do you report about someone who is missing?
accepted: their name and where they were last seen
questions.answerText: Their name and last known location
questions.why: Report anyone missing and their last known location to the person responsible for the headcount.

questions.question: Several people stand around you. What is the guide's way to make sure the emergency call happens?

options.text: Point at one person and tell them to call and report back
Wait to see whether anyone has called

questions.why: A general request makes people assume someone else has called. Assign one specific person.

questions.question: What should the caller give on an emergency call? Select all that apply.
questions.why: Give the location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards.

questions.question: The caller should hang up as soon as they have given the address.
questions.why: Stay on the line until you are told to hang up.

questions.question: Put the guide's first checks of an injured person in order.

items.text: Check that the scene is safe

questions.why: First make sure the scene is safe so you do not become a second casualty, then check responsiveness, then breathing.

questions.question: For how long do you look, listen and feel for breathing?
questions.why: The guide says to check breathing for up to 10 seconds.

questions.question: Which problems are life-threatening and come first? Select all that apply.
questions.why: Deal with life-threatening problems first: not breathing and severe bleeding.

questions.question: What is the first step to control severe bleeding?

options.text: Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth
Wash the wound under running water

questions.why: Firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or dressing is the first step.

questions.question: If the cloth soaks through, you should lift it off and replace it with a fresh one.
questions.why: Lifting the cloth releases pressure and can restart bleeding. Add more layers on top instead.

questions.question: The cloth on a bleeding wound has soaked through. What do you do?
questions.why: Do not remove the soaked cloth; add more layers on top and keep the pressure on.

questions.question: Put these bleeding care steps in a sensible order.

items.text: Keep the person lying down and warm
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth
Add layers if the cloth soaks through

questions.why: Pressure first, add layers rather than lifting, then keep the person lying down and warm and monitor them until help arrives.

questions.question: How long should a burn be cooled under cool running water?
questions.why: Cool the burn under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes.

questions.question: Which of these should you not put on a burn? Select all that apply.
questions.why: Do not use ice, butter, oils or toothpaste. Cool running water is the right treatment.

questions.question: A burn on the hand is a reason to seek medical help.
questions.why: The guide lists burns on the face, hands or genitals, large or deep burns, or any doubt, as reasons to seek medical help.

questions.question: A person does not respond but is breathing normally. What does the guide say?

options.text: Place them in the recovery position and monitor breathing
Sit them up and give them water

questions.why: If the person is breathing normally, place them in the recovery position, keep the airway open and monitor breathing.

questions.question: What device can you use, if one is available, when a person is not breathing normally?
questions.why: Use an AED if one is available and follow its prompts.

questions.question: About how fast are chest compressions given?
questions.why: The guide says hard and fast, about 100 to 120 per minute, in the centre of the chest.

questions.question: Put the parts of a handover to responders in the guide's order.
questions.why: A short, ordered handover: what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since.

questions.question: A good handover includes the name of any missing person and where they were last seen.
questions.why: The guide says to name any missing person and the last place they were seen.

questions.question: Which details belong in a handover? Select all that apply.

options.text: Your opinion of how the alarm system was installed
Any changes since you started helping

questions.why: A handover covers what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since.
